questions.q: Name the four major Sufi silsilas that established themselves in India during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods, and identify the founding figure or eponymous origin for each.
questions.a: The four major silsilas are: (1) Chishti — named after the town of Chisht in central Afghanistan; (2) Suhrawardi — named after Shaikh Shihabuddin Suhrawardi of Baghdad; (3) Qadiri — named after Shaikh Abd'ul Qadir Jilani of Baghdad; (4) Naqshbandi — named after Khwaja Bahauddin Naqshband of Bukhara. A wrong answer (e.g., confusing Chishti with a person, or omitting Naqshbandi) reveals the student memorised names without grasping the naming convention: most silsilas are named after a founding master, but Chishti is toponymic — a key distinction for board source-based questions.

questions.q: Explain why the Chishti silsila deliberately maintained distance from political power while the Suhrawardi and Naqshbandi silsilas accepted courtly positions, and how this difference affected their social base.
questions.a: The Chishtis viewed political proximity as a threat to spiritual autonomy — Nizamuddin Auliya refused land grants, saying "What have I to do with gardens and fields?" — which enhanced their moral authority among ordinary people (soldiers, slaves, artisans, Hindu jogis). Suhrawardis (e.g., Bahauddin Zakariya in Multan) accepted state offices like Shaykh al-Islam, aligning with the Sultanate's administrative needs but limiting their appeal to elites. Naqshbandis (e.g., Ahmad Sirhindi under Jahangir) actively sought Mughal patronage to enforce shari'a compliance, gaining imperial favour but alienating syncretic sections. A wrong answer that treats all silsilas as equally "apolitical" misses the strategic divergence that shaped their demographic reach — a favourite board comparison question.

questions.q: A historian finds a 14th-century Persian malfuzat text recording conversations of a Sufi shaikh who: (a) conducts sama' with Hindavi poetry, (b) runs a langar feeding all visitors regardless of religion, (c) refuses a local ruler's gift of land deeds, and (d) appoints khalifas to set up hospices in the Deccan. Which silsila does this shaikh most likely belong to, and what two pieces of evidence from the text support your identification?
questions.a: The shaikh belongs to the Chishti silsila. Evidence: (1) Use of Hindavi in sama' and adoption of local devotional forms (qawwali, langar) — the Chishtis uniquely "adapted successfully to the local environment and adopted several features of Indian devotional traditions" (NCERT). (2) Refusal of land grants — explicitly documented for Nizamuddin Auliya and Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar. A wrong attribution to Suhrawardi or Naqshbandi shows the student cannot distinguish silsila-specific praxis from generic Sufi practices; this is a classic board source-analysis trap.

questions.q: Compare the linguistic strategies of the Chishti and Qadiri silsilas in the Deccan. How did each use language to embed themselves in local communities, and what does this reveal about their respective routes of entry into the subcontinent?
questions.a: Chishtis in the Deccan (17th–18th century) composed Dakhani (Urdu variant) poems — lurinama (lullabies), shadinama (wedding songs), charkhanama (spinning-wheel songs) — sung by women during domestic chores, embedding Islam in village life through "pre-existing bhakti tradition of Kannada vachanas and Marathi abhangs." Qadiris, named after the Baghdad-based Abd'ul Qadir Jilani, spread via Arab traders and maritime networks along the Malabar coast, adopting Malayalam and matriliny; their texts (e.g., ginan in Khojaki script) served mercantile communities in Gujarat/Sindh. Chishtis entered overland with Turkic migrations and indigenised through Sufi-Bhakti dialogue; Qadiris entered via Indian Ocean trade and indigenised through merchant-community accommodation. A student who conflates the two routes misses the geography-language link that examiners test in map-based and source-based questions.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The Naqshbandi silsila's insistence on strict shari'a compliance and silent zikr (zikr-i khafi) made it less accessible to non-Muslims than the Chishti silsila, but more effective as an instrument of Mughal state ideology under Jahangir and Aurangzeb." Support your evaluation with two specific historical examples.
questions.a: The claim is largely valid. Naqshbandi exclusivity: Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i Sani) opposed Akbar's sulh-i kul, rejected sama' as bid'a, and wrote Maktubat-i Imam Rabbani asserting shari'a supremacy — limiting appeal to non-Muslims. Mughal instrumentality: Jahangir imprisoned Sirhindi briefly but later honoured him; Aurangzeb patronised Naqshbandi khanqahs and appointed their disciples to judicial posts, using their shari'a-centric authority to legitimise Islamic orthodoxy. Contrast: Chishti sama' with Hindu jogis, qawwali in Hindavi, and Jahanara's pilgrimage to Ajmer (Source 7) show cross-communal accessibility. A student who calls Naqshbandis "anti-Hindu" oversimplifies — they were pro-shari'a, which served Mughal state-building; the nuance is what distinguishes a 90+ answer.

questions.q: Construct a comparative table with four columns (Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi) and five rows: (1) Eponymous origin, (2) Key Indian centre (13th–17th c.), (3) Language of discourse, (4) State relationship, (5) Distinctive practice. Fill it using only evidence from the NCERT chapter.
questions.a:
| Silsila | Eponymous origin | Key Indian centre | Language | State relationship | Distinctive practice |
|---------|------------------|-------------------|----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Chishti | Town of Chisht, Afghanistan | Ajmer, Delhi, Ajodhan | Hindavi, Dakhani, Punjabi | Distance; accepted unsolicited grants only | Sama' (qawwali), langar, ziyarat |
| Suhrawardi | Shaikh Shihabuddin Suhrawardi, Baghdad | Multan, Uchch | Persian, Sindhi | Accepted court offices (Shaykh al-Islam) | Khalq-i khuda (serving creation) |
| Qadiri | Shaikh Abd'ul Qadir Jilani, Baghdad | Bidar, Deccan ports | Dakhani, Malayalam, Khojaki script | Merchant patronage; limited direct state ties | Ginan recitation, maritime networks |
| Naqshbandi | Khwaja Bahauddin Naqshband, Bukhara | Delhi, Sirhind | Persian, Arabic | Active Mughal alliance (Sirhindi, Miyan Mir) | Silent zikr (zikr-i khafi), shari'a enforcement |

A poorly filled table (e.g., leaving Qadiri centres blank, confusing languages) reveals the student cannot synthesise scattered textual references — a skill directly tested in board 8-marker "Compare and contrast" questions.
